common_name: Supreme Sultan Bearded Iris (Orange and Mahogany Bicolor Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Supreme Sultan is a fragrant, richly colored bicolor bearded iris bred by Keith Keppel.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Supreme Sultan, hybridized by Keith Keppel and introduced in the late 1980s, bears large, ruffled, fragrant flowers with vivid orange standards contrasting against rich mahogany-red falls, a striking bicolor pattern that earned it an Award of Merit in 1992 after an Honorable Mention in 1990. The heavily branched stalks carry numerous buds for a long bloom season. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the old woody center and replanting only firm, healthy rhizome sections.

common_name: Everything Plus Bearded Iris (1991 Dykes Medal Ruffled Blue and White Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Everything Plus is an American Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris hybridized by O. David Niswonger.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Everything Plus, registered by O. David Niswonger in 1984, carries heavily ruffled pale blue standards over white falls stitched with deep violet and finished with mustard-gold beards tipped in purple-bronze. After earning High Commendation in 1982 and 1983, an Honorable Mention in 1986, and an Award of Merit in 1988, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1991. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the old woody center.

common_name: Absolute Treasure Bearded Iris (Fragrant Sky Blue Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Absolute Treasure is a Wister Medal-winning bearded iris hybridized by Richard Tasco.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil; Absolute Treasure, registered by Richard Tasco in 2005, bears heavily ruffled, sky blue flowers with white beards tipped golden yellow and a light, sweet fragrance. It earned an Honorable Mention in 2008, an Award of Merit in 2010, and the Wister Medal in 2013. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the old woody center and replanting only firm, healthy rhizome sections.

common_name: Swank Siberian Iris (Deep Blue Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Swank is a Morgan Award-winning Siberian iris bred by Ben Hager from 'White Swirl' and 'Bluecape'.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Swank, bred by Ben Hager from 'White Swirl' crossed with 'Bluecape' and registered in 1968, bears a deep blue self flower with little signal marking, giving a clean, saturated color rare among earlier Siberian iris cultivars. It received High Commendation in 1968, an Honorable Mention in 1970, and the Morgan Award in 1973. Like other Siberian iris it tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and can go many years without division; when clumps become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Roaring Jelly Siberian Iris (Dark Violet Iris with White Veining)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Roaring Jelly is a Morgan-Wood Medal-winning Siberian iris bred by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Roaring Jelly, introduced by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks in 1992, bears very dark violet falls highlighted with fine white veining beneath nearly white standards lightly veined in lavender, a striking dark-and-light contrast that made it the top-ranked cultivar in the 2005 Siberian Iris Society Popularity Poll. It was awarded the Morgan-Wood Medal in 1999. Clumps tolerate wetter soil than bearded iris and can go many years without needing division; when crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Lion King Japanese Iris (Grape Purple Double Iris with White Center)

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light partial shade; Japanese iris are heavier water users than Siberian or bearded iris and perform best at a pond margin or in a bog-like bed that never fully dries out during the growing season.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light partial shade. Lion King, a 1996 introduction from Bob Bauer and John Coble, produces huge, ruffled, double flowers up to 8 inches across with six falls showing wide grape-purple borders around pure white centers and a small yellow signal. It earned an American Iris Society Award of Merit in 2001 and the Payne Medal in 2003. Japanese iris demand consistently moist, acidic soil through the growing season and decline quickly if allowed to dry out; a pond margin or heavily irrigated bed suits them best. Divide clumps every three to four years in early fall to maintain vigor and bloom quality.
